title: No-Knead Bread
description: Jim Lahey's famous no-knead loaf from the New York Times: a wet dough, an overnight rise, and a screaming-hot covered pot stand in for kneading. The printout carries a handwritten substitution of active dry yeast for instant.
ingredients: 3 cups all-purpose or bread flour, more for dusting
1/3 teaspoon active dry yeast (handwritten substitution for the printed 1/4 teaspoon instant yeast)
Cornmeal or wheat bran as needed
instructions: In a large bowl combine flour, yeast and salt. Add 1 5/8 cups water, and stir until blended; dough will be shaggy and sticky. Cover bowl with plastic wrap. Let dough rest at least 12 hours, preferably about 18, at warm room temperature, about 70 degrees.

Dough is ready when its surface is dotted with bubbles. Lightly flour a work surface and place dough on it; sprinkle it with a little more flour and fold it over on itself once or twice. Cover loosely with plastic wrap and let rest about 15 minutes.

Using just enough flour to keep dough from sticking to work surface or to your fingers, gently and quickly shape dough into a ball. Generously coat a cotton towel (not terry cloth) with flour, wheat bran or cornmeal; put dough seam side down on towel and dust with more flour, bran or cornmeal. Cover with another cotton towel and let rise for about 2 hours. When it is ready, dough will be more than double in size and will not readily spring back when poked with a finger.

At least a half-hour before dough is ready, heat oven to 450 degrees. Put a 6- to 8-quart heavy covered pot (cast iron, enamel, Pyrex or ceramic) in oven as it heats. When dough is ready, carefully remove pot from oven. Slide your hand under towel and turn dough over into pot, seam side up; it may look like a mess, but that is O.K. Shake pan once or twice if dough is unevenly distributed; it will straighten out as it bakes. Cover with lid and bake 30 minutes, then remove lid and bake another 15 to 30 minutes, until loaf is beautifully browned. Cool on a rack.
notes: *Paul Bread:* the back of a companion printout carries the handwritten label "პური / Paul Bread" — kept with this recipe.
*Yeast:* the printed 1/4 teaspoon instant yeast is crossed out; the handwritten note reads "1/3 teaspoon active dry yeast."
*Yield:* one 1 1/2-pound loaf.

title: Buttermilk Pancakes II
description: Light, fluffy buttermilk pancakes from a well-used Allrecipes printout; keeping the wet and dry mixtures separate until the last minute is the key to the texture. Makes 12 servings.
instructions: In a large bowl, combine flour, sugar, baking powder, baking soda, and salt. In a separate bowl, beat together buttermilk, milk, eggs and melted butter. Keep the two mixtures separate until you are ready to cook.
Heat a lightly oiled griddle or frying pan over medium high heat. You can flick water across the surface and if it beads up and sizzles, it's ready!

Pour the wet mixture into the dry mixture, using a wooden spoon or fork to blend. Stir until it's just blended together. Do not over stir! Pour or scoop the batter onto the griddle, using approximately 1/2 cup for each pancake. Brown on both sides and serve hot.
notes: *Technique:* do not overmix; a slightly lumpy batter keeps the pancakes tender.

INGREDIENTS:

3 tablespoons white sugar
3 teaspoons baking powder
1 1/2 teaspoons baking soda
3/4 teaspoon salt
3 cups buttermilk
1/2 cup milk
3 eggs
1/3 cup butter, melted

DIRECTIONS:

2. Heat a lightly oiled griddle or frying pan over medium high heat. You can flick water across the surface and if it beads up and sizzles, it's ready!
3. Pour the wet mixture into the dry mixture, using a wooden spoon or fork to blend. Stir until it's just blended together. Do not over stir! Pour or scoop the batter onto the griddle, using approximately 1/2 cup for each pancake. Brown on both sides and serve hot.

title: 2-Hour Fastest No Knead Bread
description: Jenny Jones's quick Dutch-oven no-knead loaf from JennyCanCook.com. Extra yeast and hot water cut the usual overnight rest down to a single hour, for a crusty loaf in about two hours start to finish.
ingredients: 3 cups (360–390 g / 12 3/4 ounces) bread flour or all purpose flour (aerate flour before measuring)
2 teaspoons instant or RapidRise yeast (1 packet / 7 g)
About 2 tablespoons extra flour for shaping
instructions: Combine flour, 2 teaspoons yeast, and salt in a large bowl. Stir in water until it's well combined.
Cover with plastic wrap and let stand at room temperature for 1 hour.
After 40 minutes, place a 3 to 6-quart Dutch oven with lid in a cold oven and preheat to 450°F.
After the dough has rested for the hour, place it on a well-floured surface and sprinkle with a little flour. Using a scraper, fold dough over 10–12 times and shape into a rough ball.
Place in a parchment paper-lined bowl (not wax paper) and cover with a towel or another bowl. Let stand on counter top for 15 minutes.

After 15 minutes, carefully, using oven gloves, lift the parchment paper with the dough and transfer gently into the hot pot (the dough sits inside a parchment "basket" inside the pot). Cover and bake for 30 minutes.
After 30 minutes, remove lid and parchment paper. Return, uncovered, to oven and bake 10–15 more minutes. Let it cool at least 15 minutes before slicing.
notes: *Flour weight:* The card notes 1 cup = 120 g standard, but the author measures 125–130 g per cup.
*Timing:* Prep 3 minutes, cook 40 minutes, total 2 hours; makes one loaf.

title: Mom's Zucchini Bread
description: The five-star Allrecipes classic: a moist cinnamon-vanilla zucchini quick bread with walnuts, making two loaves. Freezes well and keeps in the refrigerator for weeks.
instructions: Grease and flour two 8 x 4 inch pans. Preheat oven to 325 degrees F (165 degrees C).
Sift flour, salt, baking powder, soda, and cinnamon together in a bowl.

Beat eggs, oil, vanilla, and sugar together in a large bowl. Add sifted ingredients to the creamed mixture, and beat well. Stir in zucchini and nuts until well combined. Pour batter into prepared pans.
Bake for 40 to 60 minutes, or until tester inserted in the center comes out clean. Cool in pan on rack for 20 minutes. Remove bread from pan, and cool completely.
notes: *Timing:* Prep 20 minutes, cook 1 hour; 24 servings (two loaves).
original:
Mom's Zucchini Bread — allrecipes.com

Rated: 5 stars
Submitted By: v monte
Prep Time: 20 Minutes
Cook Time: 1 Hour
Ready In: 1 Hour 40 Minutes
Servings: 24

"Really, really good and moist- my kids eat it as quickly as I can make it. Bread will freeze well, and keep in refrigerator for weeks."

INGREDIENTS:

3 cups all-purpose flour
1 teaspoon salt
1 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon baking powder
3 teaspoons ground cinnamon
3 eggs
1 cup vegetable oil
2 1/4 cups white sugar
3 teaspoons vanilla extract
2 cups grated zucchini
1 cup chopped walnuts

DIRECTIONS:

1. Grease and flour two 8 x 4 inch pans. Preheat oven to 325 degrees F (165 degrees C).
2. Sift flour, salt, baking powder, soda, and cinnamon together in a bowl.
3. Beat eggs, oil, vanilla, and sugar together in a large bowl. Add sifted ingredients to the creamed mixture, and beat well. Stir in zucchini and nuts until well combined. Pour batter into prepared pans.
4. Bake for 40 to 60 minutes, or until tester inserted in the center comes out clean. Cool in pan on rack for 20 minutes. Remove bread from pan, and completely cool.

title: Dumpling Dough with Boiling Water (Super)
description: This traditional "choux" pastry technique for Russian _pelmeni_ or _vareniki_ uses boiling water to partially gelatinize the starch in the flour. This process results in an exceptionally elastic and pliable dough that can be rolled very thin without tearing, ensuring the dumplings remain intact and tender during the boiling process.
instructions: Add the salt to the egg and beat with a fork. Then add 3 cups of flour and a spoonful of vegetable oil; mix well. Add 1 cup of boiling water and stir with a spoon, then knead by hand (add a little flour if necessary).
notes: *Temperature Control:* Use water that has just reached a rolling boil to ensure the flour properly scalds, which gives the dough its signature elasticity.
*Safety:* Start mixing with a spoon immediately after adding the boiling water to avoid burns; only switch to hand-kneading once the temperature is comfortable to touch.

*Resting:* Although not mentioned in the original note, allowing the dough to rest for 20–30 minutes under a bowl or plastic wrap will significantly improve its texture and make it easier to roll out.

description: Imeretian Khachapuri is a cornerstone of Georgian culinary tradition, celebrated for its perfect balance of salty, crumbly Imeretian cheese and elastic Sulguni. The key to a successful khachapuri lies in achieving a high-hydration, soft dough that is handled gently to preserve its airy structure, ensuring a tender crust that complements the rich, molten cheese filling.

notes: *Temperature Control:* Ensure the water is lukewarm (not hot) to avoid killing the yeast; keep the rising dough in a draft-free, warm spot.
*Handling:* Use oil on your hands rather than excessive flour to manage stickiness, which keeps the dough soft and light. The dough will take roughly 40 - 45 minutes to rise.
*Cheese Ratio:* For the best results, use a 2:1 ratio of Imeretian cheese to Sulguni to achieve the traditional flavor profile and texture.
*Alternative Cheeses:* If Imeretian and Sulguni cheeses are hard to come by, you may use mexican and mazarella cheese as substitutes (respectively).

title: Vareniki Dough (Dumpling Dough)
description: This recipe utilizes the "scalded dough" technique, a staple of Eastern European culinary tradition. By pouring boiling water directly into the flour, the starches partially gelatinize, resulting in an exceptionally elastic and pliable dough that can be rolled paper-thin without tearing and maintains a silky, tender texture after boiling.
instructions: Make a well in the sifted flour.
Pour the boiling hot water into the center.
Add a teaspoon of salt and let the mixture cool slightly.
Add the oil, stir, and then add 1 or 2 eggs.
Knead the dough.
Add flour bit by bit until the dough is ready.
Combine the boiling water, oil, and salt.
Add a small amount of flour to the hot mixture to cool it down, then add the egg.
Gradually add the remaining 280–300g of flour.
Let the dough rest for 30 minutes.
notes: Ensure the water is truly at a rolling boil when added to achieve the proper "scalded" starch consistency. Always allow the hot water/flour mixture to cool slightly before adding the eggs to prevent them from scrambling. Letting the dough rest for at least 30 minutes is crucial for relaxing the gluten, making it much easier to roll out.

title: Russian Pirozhki with Scalded Yeast Dough (Yields 30)
description: This traditional recipe utilizes the "scalded" (zavarnoy) method, where boiling water is poured over a small portion of the flour to gelatinize the starches. This technique creates a dough that is exceptionally soft, easy to handle without sticking, and results in a finished pastry that stays tender and fresh much longer than standard yeast breads.
instructions: *Stage I:* Combine flour (3 tbsp), vegetable oil (3 tbsp), sugar (1 tbsp), and salt (1 tsp). Pour the boiling water over the mixture. Mix thoroughly and let it cool until it is warm to the touch.
*Stage II:* To the warm mixture, add the yeast and 1 cup of warm water. Gradually incorporate the 500g of flour. Knead the dough until smooth.

*Shaping and Cooking:* Form the dough into small balls. Let the balls rest for 5–10 minutes. Shape the pirozhki with your desired filling and fry them in a skillet with oil. Alternatively, they can be baked in the oven.
notes: The most critical step is ensuring the scalded flour mixture has cooled down to a lukewarm temperature before adding the yeast; if the mixture is too hot, it will deactivate the yeast and the dough will not rise. For a perfect fry, ensure the oil is hot before adding the pirozhki to prevent them from becoming greasy.

description: This recipe utilizes the traditional "chopped dough" technique, where butter is worked into flour to create distinct layers, resulting in a signature flaky and tender crust. title: Adjarian Khachapuri
description: This recipe details the preparation of a traditional Georgian Khachapuri, a staple cheese-filled bread. The core science of this recipe relies on a high-hydration, enriched yeast dough that is briefly rested to develop gluten elasticity, paired with a high-heat bake (220-250°C) to ensure a rapid rise and a characteristic golden, soft crust that encases the molten cheese interior.
ingredients: Dough needs to rise at least 40 minutes
Warm water: 1/2 pitcher (300 ml water for 2 khachapuri. Add some milk)
Water: A small amount to loosen the cheese mixture
instructions: Mix the warm water, yeast, salt, sugar, and flour. Knead the dough until it is smooth and soft. Incorporate the oil at the end of kneading. Let the dough rest and rise for approximately 40 minutes.
Once the dough rises, dust the table with some flour and pinch off enough dough for one portion, about the size of a fist.
With the circular motion, round the dough into a ball, cover it up and let it rest for 10 minutes
Once rested, flatten the ball in the middle. Leave the edges thick and puffy.
Turn it over, stretch it into an oval shape. Pick it up and lay it down by folding the edges towards the center, pinch the opposite sides, creating a boat shape
Gently stretch it from the bottom towards the sides, keep shaping it like a boat
Dust some flour on the baking sheet
Add grated cheese, some sulguni on top.
Bake at 220-250 Celsius
When it's half way baked, scrape the dough off the sides with a fork
Add an egg yolk and leave in the oven for another minute
notes: *Temperature:* Ensure the oven is very hot (at least 220°C) before sliding the bread in; this high heat is vital for the dough's "oven spring."
*Texture:* The filling should be moist but not runny; add water to the cheese gradually until it reaches a spreadable consistency.
*Elasticity:* If the dough resists flattening, let it rest for 5 minutes to allow the gluten to relax.

description: This manual method for laminating dough creates the classic "puff" effect through mechanical layering. By alternating rolling, folding, and chilling, you create dozens of alternating layers of dough and fat; during baking, the moisture in the fat turns to steam, forcing the layers apart to create a light, airy, and crisp texture.
ingredients: No ingredients are listed on this page; these instructions are for the final preparation of the dough.
instructions: Place the dough in the refrigerator for 1 hour, or in the freezer for 15-20 minutes.

Continue the process of rolling and folding. Roll it out into a strip again and fold it in the exact same manner.
Wrap the dough in plastic wrap and place it back in the refrigerator for 1 hour, or in the freezer for 15-20 minutes.
Repeat this entire cycle twice to ensure the finished pastry turns out light and flaky!
notes: Temperature control is the most critical factor for success. If the fat (butter) becomes too soft or melts into the flour, the layers will fuse and the pastry will not rise. If the dough starts to feel sticky or elastic while rolling, return it to the freezer immediately for 10 minutes before continuing.

title: Adjarian Khachapuri
description: Adjarian Khachapuri is a signature boat-shaped Georgian bread traditionally filled with a mixture of Imeretian and Sulguni cheeses. The dough's elasticity comes from a simple yeast-based foundation, while the high-heat baking process creates a crisp exterior and a molten, cheesy center that is typically finished with a fresh egg yolk and a pat of butter.
instructions: Dissolve 10g of yeast with sugar.
Add 300ml warm water, 5-7g salt, 3-4 tablespoons of oil, and 450-500g of flour.
Knead the dough and let it rest for 30-40 minutes.
Once the dough has risen, sprinkle flour on the work surface and remove the dough from the bowl.
Using gentle hand movements, take one handful of dough for each khachapuri.
Shape the portions into rounds and let them rest for another 10 minutes.
Flatten the dough by hand, ensuring the edges remain thick to form the structural walls.
Fold along the width and stretch it out to form the boat shape.
Mash the cheese and curd cheese together with one egg.
Place the filling in the center, fold the sides inward, and pull up the edges at the ends to secure the shape.
Bake at 220°C (430°F).
notes: Use lukewarm water (around 100°F) to ensure the yeast activates without dying.
Avoid over-kneading the dough; it should remain soft and slightly airy for a light crust.
For the boat shape, leave the perimeter of the dough circle significantly thicker than the center before folding.

title: Adjarian Khachapuri
description: Khachapuri is Georgia's quintessential cheese bread, a staple of national identity where the interplay of soft, yeasted dough and melted cheese is paramount. The secret to its texture lies in a high hydration dough enriched with margarine, which creates a tender crumb that perfectly complements the salty, elastic cheese filling.
ingredients: Approximately 8 cups of flour (add as much as the dough absorbs)
instructions: Take 1 liter of warm water and mix well with 1 tablespoon of yeast, 1 tablespoon of sugar, 100g of margarine, and 1 teaspoon of salt.
Add the flour (about 8 cups), add just enough so that the dough is not too hard.
Let the dough rest for 1/2 hour.
Once it has risen, move the dough to a table and cut it into round balls (this amount makes about 10–11 pieces).
Let these balls sit until they rise again, then flatten them and give them their final shape.
Prepare the filling by mixing the cheese with a little water and a beaten egg.
When the bread is half-baked, you may pour an individual egg into each one (for Adjaruli style).
notes: Success depends on dough consistency; it should remain soft and pliable rather than stiff, so add flour gradually. For the filling, adding a splash of water to the cheese ensures it remains creamy and doesn't dry out during the baking process.

description: This recipe utilizes the "zavarnoy" (scalded) method, where boiling water is used to gelatinize a portion of the flour's starch. This technique results in a dough that is exceptionally soft, elastic, and easy to work with, while ensuring the finished pastries stay fresh and tender for a longer period.

title: Beef Bourguignon
description: Ina Garten's Barefoot Contessa take on the Burgundian classic: chuck beef seared with bacon, flamed with Cognac, and braised in a full bottle of red wine, served over garlic-rubbed toasted bread. Printed from Food Network; serves 6.
ingredients: 8 ounces dry cured center cut applewood smoked bacon, diced
2 1/2 pounds chuck beef cut into 1-inch cubes
1 pound carrots, sliced diagonally into 1-inch chunks
1 (750 ml.) bottle good dry red wine such as Cote du Rhone or Pinot Noir
1 teaspoon fresh thyme leaves (1/2 teaspoon dried)
4 tablespoons unsalted butter at room temperature, divided
1 pound fresh mushrooms, stems discarded, caps thickly sliced
Country bread or sourdough, toasted or grilled and rubbed with garlic clove
instructions: Preheat the oven to 250 degrees F.

Heat the olive oil in a large Dutch oven. Add the bacon and cook over medium heat for 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the bacon is lightly browned. Remove the bacon with a slotted spoon to a large plate.

Dry the beef cubes with paper towels and then sprinkle them with salt and pepper. In batches in single layers, sear the beef in the hot oil for 3 to 5 minutes, turning to brown on all sides. Remove the seared cubes to the plate with the bacon and continue searing until all the beef is browned. Set aside.

Toss the carrots, and onions, 1 tablespoon of salt and 2 teaspoons of pepper in the fat in the pan and cook for 10 to 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the onions are lightly browned. Add the garlic and cook for 1 more minute. Add the Cognac, stand back, and ignite with a match to burn off the alcohol. Put the meat and bacon back into the pot with the juices. Add the bottle of wine plus enough beef broth to almost cover the meat. Add the tomato paste and thyme. Bring to a simmer, cover the pot with a tight-fitting lid and place it in the oven for about 1 1/4 hours or until the meat and vegetables are very tender when pierced with a fork.

Combine 2 tablespoons of butter and the flour with a fork and stir into the stew. Add the frozen onions. Saute the mushrooms in 2 tablespoons of butter for 10 minutes until lightly browned and then add to the stew. Bring the stew to a boil on top of the stove, then lower the heat and simmer for 15 minutes. Season to taste.
To serve, toast the bread in the toaster or oven. Rub each slice on 1 side with a cut clove of garlic. For each serving, spoon the stew over a slice of bread and sprinkle with parsley.

NYT Cooking — 12/3/2019

Old-Fashioned Beef Stew
By Molly O'Neill

YIELD 4 servings
TIME 2 hours 30 minutes

This classic stick-to-your-ribs stew is the ideal project for a chilly weekend. Beef, onion, carrots, potatoes and red wine come together in cozy harmony. If you are feeding a crowd, good news: It doubles (or triples) beautifully.

2 large baking potatoes, peeled and cut into 3/4-inch cubes
2 teaspoons salt

Step 1
Combine the flour and pepper in a bowl, add the beef and toss to coat well. Heat 3 teaspoons of the oil in a large pot. Add the beef a few pieces at a time; do not overcrowd. Remove the beef from the pot and add the vinegar and wine. Cook over medium-high heat, scraping the pan with a wooden spoon to loosen any browned bits. Add the beef, beef broth and bay leaves. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a slow simmer.

Cover and cook, skimming broth from time to time, until the beef is tender, about 1 1/2 hours. Add the onions and carrots and simmer, covered, for 10 minutes. title: Ina Garten's Unforgettable Beef Stew
description: A printout from Veggies By Candlelight of Ina Garten's red wine-marinated beef stew, oven-braised with carrots, potatoes, sun-dried tomatoes, and rosemary. The card has hand-strikethroughs on the red wine and the mushrooms.
ingredients: 2 1/2 pounds good quality beef chuck, cubed into \~1 1/2" pieces
1 bottle of good red wine (struck through on the card)
2 cups flour (all-purpose, whole wheat pastry, or oat)
1 pound carrots, peeled and cut diagonally into 1 1/2" chunks
1/2 pound white mushrooms, stems discarded and halved (struck through on the card)

instructions: Marinate the beef: Place the beef in a bowl with red wine, garlic, and bay leaves. Marinate overnight in the refrigerator.
The next day, preheat the oven to 300°F.
In a medium bowl, combine the flour, 1 Tbsp salt, and pepper.
Lift the beef out of the marinade with a slotted spoon, discard the bay leaves and garlic, saving the marinade. In batches, dredge the beef cubes in the flour mix and shake off the excess.

Heat a glug of olive oil in a large pot and brown half the beef over medium heat for 5–7 minutes, turning to brown evenly. Place the beef in a large oven-proof Dutch oven and brown the remaining beef, adding oil as necessary. Place all the beef in the Dutch oven.

Prep the veggies: In a large pot, heat another glug of oil, then add the onions, carrots, mushrooms, and potatoes. Cook for 10 minutes over medium heat, stirring occasionally. Add the garlic and cook a couple more minutes.
Place all the vegetables into the Dutch oven over the beef.

Add 2 1/2 cups of the reserved marinade to the empty pot and cook over high heat to deglaze, scraping up the brown bits with a wooden spoon. Add the stock, rosemary, sun-dried tomatoes, Worcestershire sauce, 1/2 Tbsp salt, and 2 tsp pepper.
Pour the sauce over the meat and vegetables and bring to a simmer over medium heat on the stove.
Cover the pot and bake about 2 hours, until meat and vegetables are tender, stirring once. If the stew boils rather than simmers, lower the heat to 250 or 275°F.

NYT Cooking

Shakshuka With Feta
By Melissa Clark

YIELD 4 to 6 servings
TIME 50 minutes

Shakshuka may be at the apex of eggs-for-dinner recipes, though in Israel it is breakfast food, a bright, spicy start to the day with a pile of pita or challah served on the side. (It also makes excellent brunch or lunch food.) It's a one-skillet recipe of eggs baked in a tomato-red pepper sauce spiced with cumin, paprika and cayenne. First you make that sauce, which comes together fairly quickly on top of the stove, then you gently crack each of the eggs into the pan, nestling them into the sauce. The pan is moved into the oven to finish. Shakshuka originated in North Africa, and like many great dishes there are as many versions as there are cooks who have embraced it. This one strays from more traditional renditions by adding crumbled feta cheese, which softens into creamy nuggets in the oven's heat.

INGREDIENTS
3 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil
1 large onion, halved and thinly sliced
1 large red bell pepper, seeded and thinly sliced
3 garlic cloves, thinly sliced
1 teaspoon ground cumin
1 teaspoon sweet paprika
1/8 teaspoon ground cayenne, or to taste
1 (28-ounce) can whole plum tomatoes with their juices, coarsely chopped
3/4 teaspoon kosher salt, plus more as needed
1/4 teaspoon black pepper, plus more as needed
5 ounces feta, crumbled (about 1 1/4 cups)
6 large eggs
Chopped cilantro, for serving
Hot sauce, for serving

PREPARATION
Step 1
Heat oven to 375 degrees. Heat oil in a large skillet over medium-low. Add onion and bell pepper. Cook gently until very soft, about 20 minutes. Add garlic and cook until tender, 1 to 2 minutes; stir in cumin, paprika and cayenne, and cook 1 minute. Pour in tomatoes and season with 3/4 teaspoon salt and 1/4 teaspoon pepper; simmer until tomatoes have thickened, about 10 minutes. Taste and add more salt and pepper if needed. Stir in crumbled feta.

Step 2
Gently crack eggs into skillet over tomatoes. Season eggs with salt and pepper. Transfer skillet to oven and bake until eggs are just set, 7 to 10 minutes. Sprinkle with cilantro and serve with hot sauce.

title: Fresh Huevos Rancheros
description: A vegetarian Mexican breakfast of fried eggs on tortillas spread with quick refried beans, topped with warm salsa and fresh pico de gallo. Printed from Cookie and Kate; yields 4 hearty but modest servings of one tortilla and egg each.
ingredients: 1 can (15 ounces) black beans or pinto beans, rinsed and drained, or 1 1/2 cups cooked beans
Freshly ground black pepper, to taste
1 1/2 cups (12 ounces) of your favorite red salsa, homemade or jarred
Optional garnishes: crumbled Cotija or feta cheese, sliced avocado, additional chopped cilantro and/or hot sauce
instructions: To prepare the pico de gallo: In a medium bowl, combine the tomatoes, onion, cilantro, lime juice, and salt. Stir to combine, then set the bowl aside for later.

To cook the beans: In a small saucepan over medium heat, warm the olive oil until shimmering. Add the onions and salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the onions have softened and are turning translucent, about 3 to 6 minutes.

Add the cumin and cook, stirring constantly, until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Pour in the drained beans and water. Stir, cover and cook for 5 minutes. Reduce the heat to low, then remove the lid and use a potato masher or the back of a fork to mash up about at least half of the beans. Continue to cook the beans, uncovered, stirring often, for 2 to 3 more minutes, until thickened.

Remove the pot from the heat and stir in the pepper and lime juice. Taste and add more salt, pepper or lime juice if necessary. If the beans seem dry, add a very small splash of water and stir to combine. Cover until you're ready to serve.

Meanwhile, warm the salsa. Pour the salsa into a medium saucepan over medium heat. Bring the salsa to a simmer, stirring occasionally, and then reduce the heat to low until you're ready to serve. (Or warm the salsa in a bowl in the microwave.)

In a small skillet over medium heat, warm each tortilla individually, flipping as necessary. Spread the black bean mixture over each tortilla and place each tortilla on an individual plate. If using Jack cheese, sprinkle it over the tortillas. Set aside.

To fry the eggs: In the same skillet over medium heat, pour in 1 teaspoon olive oil and wait until it's shimmering. Carefully crack an egg and pour it into the skillet without breaking the yolk. Fry the egg, lifting and tilting the pan occasionally to redistribute the oil, until the whites are set and the yolk is cooked to your preferred level of doneness. Place the fried egg on top of a prepared tortilla and repeat with the remaining eggs.

Spoon about one-fourth of the warmed salsa across each dish, avoiding the egg yolk. Use a slotted spoon or fork to do the same with the pico de gallo, leaving the messy tomato juices behind. Sprinkle with freshly ground black pepper and add any additional garnishes you might like.
Serve immediately. If you don't use up all of your beans, leftovers are a great dip for tortilla chips.
notes: *If tomatoes aren't in season:* skip the pico de gallo and top with chopped cilantro and avocado slices instead.
*Leftovers tip:* store the components separately and fry the tortilla and egg just before serving.

INSTRUCTIONS
1. To prepare the pico de gallo: In a medium bowl, combine the tomatoes, onion, cilantro, lime juice, and salt. Stir to combine, then set the bowl aside for later.
2. To cook the beans: In a small saucepan over medium heat, warm the olive oil until shimmering. Add the onions and salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the onions have softened and are turning translucent, about 3 to 6 minutes.
3. Add the cumin and cook, stirring constantly, until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Pour in the drained beans and water. Stir, cover and cook for 5 minutes. Reduce the heat to low, then remove the lid and use a potato masher or the back of a fork to mash up about at least half of the beans. Continue to cook the beans, uncovered, stirring often, for 2 to 3 more minutes, until thickened.
4. Remove the pot from the heat and stir in the pepper and lime juice. Taste and add more salt, pepper or lime juice if necessary. If the beans seem dry, add a very small splash of water and stir to combine. Cover until you're ready to serve.
5. Meanwhile, warm the salsa. Pour the salsa into a medium saucepan over medium heat. Bring the salsa to a simmer, stirring occasionally, and then reduce the heat to low until you're ready to serve. (Or, warm the salsa in a bowl in the microwave—it won't condense as much but it'll work!)
6. In a small skillet over medium heat, warm each tortilla individually, flipping as necessary. Spread the black bean mixture over each tortilla and place each tortilla on an individual plate. If using Jack cheese, sprinkle it over the tortillas. Set aside.
7. To fry the eggs: In the same skillet over medium heat, pour in 1 teaspoon olive oil and wait until it's shimmering. Carefully crack an egg and pour it into the skillet without breaking the yolk. Fry the egg, lifting and tilting the pan occasionally to redistribute the oil, until the whites are set and the yolk is cooked to your preferred level of doneness. Place the fried egg on top of a prepared tortilla and repeat with the remaining eggs.
8. Spoon about one-fourth of the warmed salsa across each dish, avoiding the egg yolk. Use a slotted spoon or fork to do the same with the pico de gallo, leaving the messy tomato juices behind. Sprinkle with freshly ground black pepper and add any additional garnishes you might like.
9. Serve immediately. If you don't use up all of your beans, leftovers are a great dip for tortilla chips.

NOTES
*If tomatoes aren't in season: You might want to skip the pico de gallo, and top your dish with some chopped cilantro and avocado slices instead.
Leftovers tip: If you won't be consuming all four servings of this dish right away, store the individual components separately and fry your tortilla and egg just before serving.

instructions: Preheat a two-sided electric griddle on medium-high to high for about 20 minutes, or preheat the oven to 300 degrees and preheat a cast-iron skillet on top of the stove for about 5 minutes. title: Slow-Roasted Crispy Pork Belly
description: Nagi's RecipeTin Eats method for pork belly slow-roasted in a foil "box" so it confits in its own fat, then blasted at high heat for crackling. The three techniques: do not score the skin, low heat then high heat, and keep the pork level with balls of foil.
ingredients: 1 kg / 2 lb pork belly with skin on, NOT scored; 3–3.5 cm / 1.2–1.6" thick, even thickness with flat, unwrinkled skin, preferably not vac-packed
1/2 tsp fennel powder / ground fennel seeds (optional)
1 tsp salt, cooking/kosher salt (or 7/8 tsp table salt), divided
See in post for more sauce options
instructions: Dry skin overnight: Place pork belly on a plate. Pat skin dry with paper towels. Leave uncovered in fridge overnight to dry out the skin. (If you don't have time, pat the skin dry as best you can.)
Preheat oven to 140°C/285°F (120°C fan).
Season flesh: Drizzle flesh (only) with 1 tsp oil. Sprinkle over 1/2 tsp salt, the pepper and fennel powder. Rub all over the flesh, including the sides, getting into all the cracks and crevices.

Wrap in foil: Place 2 pieces of foil on a work surface. Put the belly in the middle, skin side up. Fold the sides in to enclose the belly, forming an open box, pinching corners to seal tightly and make it as snug as possible. Place meat on a tray.
Season skin: Pat skin dry with paper towels. Rub with 1/2 tsp oil, then sprinkle remaining 1/2 tsp salt evenly all over the skin surface, edge to edge.

Slow roast 2 1/2 hours: Place in the oven and roast for 2 1/2 hours. After 1 1/2 hours, remove and tighten the foil (pork will have shrunk), and continue cooking. This keeps the pork fat level high and the flesh protected so it stays moist.
Increase heat: Remove pork from oven, then increase heat to 240°C/465°F (all oven types).

Level pork: Remove pork from foil and place on a rack set over a tray (rack is best, but optional). Use scrunched-up balls of foil stuffed under the pork to prop it up so the skin surface is as level and horizontal as possible.

30 minutes on high heat: Place the pork back in the oven for 30 minutes, rotating after 15 minutes as needed, until the crackling is deep golden, puffy and crispy all over. If some patches brown faster, protect with foil patches.
Rest 10 minutes: Remove pork from oven. Rest for 10 minutes before slicing.
Serving: Slice into 2 cm / 4/5"-thick slices using a serrated knife. Pictured with Apple Sauce and Vermouth Jus and a side of Cauliflower Puree.
notes: *Pork belly:* Avoid vac-packed and pre-scored bellies; wrinkly or scored skin gives rubbery patches. If vac-packed, the overnight fridge drying is strongly recommended.
*Storage:* Keeps 3–5 days. Separate the crackling to reheat: meat in the microwave, crackling in a hot oven.
original:
Slow-Roasted Crispy Pork Belly

Recipe video above. This is a pork belly that's slow-roasted so the fat renders and cooks the belly confit-style in its own fat. The result? Ridiculously juicy, impossibly tender yet still-sliceable meat, crowned with the most amazing crispy crackling of your life. It comes down to three simple, game-changing techniques: 1. Do NOT score the skin; 2. Low heat followed by high heat; 3. Keep the pork level using balls of foil.

Perfect meat, perfect crackling ... Every. Single. Time! (Read the post for all the details on how to do it right!)

5 from 138 votes

Prep Time: 5 mins
Cook Time: 3 hrs
Drying skin in fridge: 1 d

Course: Main   Cuisine: Western
Keyword: Crispy pork belly, pork belly, pork belly crackling, slow roasted pork belly
Servings: 4 - 5 people   Calories: 1313cal   Author: Nagi

Ingredients

* 1kg / 2 lb pork belly with skin on , NOT SCORED. Look for 3 - 3.5cm / 1.2 - 1.6" thick, even thickness with flat, unwrinkled skin, preferably not vac-packed (Note 1)
* 1 1/2 tsp olive oil , divided
* 1/2 tsp fennel powder / ground fennel seeds , optional, Note 3
* 1 tsp salt , cooking/kosher salt (or 7/8 tsp table salt), divided
* 1/4 tsp black pepper

For serving (as pictured in post):
* Apple Sauce
* Vermouth Jus
* Cauliflower Puree , (Note 2)
* See in post for more Sauce options

Instructions

1. Dry skin overnight: Place pork belly on a plate. Pat skin dry with paper towels. Leave uncovered in fridge overnight to dry out the skin. (If you don't have time, pat the skin dry as best you can).
2. Preheat oven to 140°C/285°F (120°C fan).
3. Season flesh: Drizzle flesh (only) with 1 tsp oil. Sprinkle over 1/2 tsp salt, the pepper and fennel powder. Rub all over the flesh, including on the sides, being sure you get right into all the cracks and crevices.
4. Wrap in foil: Place 2 pieces of foil on a work surface. Put the belly in middle of foil, skin side up. Fold the sides in to enclose the belly, forming an open box, pinching corners to seal tightly and make it as snug as possible. Place meat on a tray.
5. Season skin: Pat skin dry with paper towels. Rub with 1/2 tsp oil then sprinkle remaining 1/2 tsp salt evenly all over the skin surface, from edge to edge.
6. Slow roast 2 1/2 hours: Place in the oven and roast for 2 1/2 hours. After 1 1/2 hours, remove and tighten the foil (pork will have shrunk), and continue cooking. This keeps the pork fat level up as high as possible, and the flesh protected so it stays moist.
7. Increase heat: Remove pork from oven, then increase heat to 240°C/465°F (all oven types).
8. Level pork: Remove pork from foil and place on a rack set over a tray (using rack is best, but optional). Use scrunched up balls of foil stuffed under pork to prop up so the skin surface is as level and horizontal as possible (see photos in post).
9. 30 minutes on high heat! Place the pork back in the oven for 30 minutes, rotating after 15 minutes as needed, until the crackling is deep golden, puffy and crispy all over. If some patches are browning faster, protect with foil patches.
10. Rest 10 minutes: Remove pork from oven. Rest for 10 minutes before slicing.
11. Serving: Slice into 2cm / 4/5"-thick slices using a serrated knife. Pictured in post with Apple Sauce and Vermouth Jus, with a side of Cauliflower Puree (Note 2)! See directions in post for how to plate it up as pictured (fine dining style!), as well as a list of more sauce options.

Notes
1. Pork Belly - It's best to get one that has not been vacuum-packed. Vac-packed means the skin has been soaking in juices for who-knows-how-long, and the crackling won't be as good (although we can still get it crispy using this recipe method!) If your belly is vac-packed, I really recommend doing the overnight drying uncovered in the fridge.

Look for a piece with flat, even skin as wrinkly skin doesn't crackle as well (in the ridges, because heat can't get to it as well).

Also, do NOT get one that is scored. It is a plain fact that you do NOT need to score for perfect crackling! All too often, butchers do poor scoring jobs and pierce through the fat into the flesh. Even the tiniest prick will cause meat juices to bubble up onto the skin and you'll end up with rubbery patches.

See in post for further information on what to look for when purchasing your pork belly.

2. Cauliflower Puree pictured in post is my Cauliflower Mash recipe which I pureed more thoroughly to make it as smooth as possible.

3. Fennel powder - This is ground fennel seeds. Fennel is a classic pairing with pork. Fennel powder gives a subtle, floral, aniseed flavouring to the pork meat. You can grind your own powder: Grind 1 tsp of lightly toasted fennel seeds in a mortar and pestle or spice grinder to yield 1/2 tsp fennel powder. If you don't have any fennel powder or seeds, you can leave it out.

4. Storage and reheating - Pork belly keeps and reheats well. Keep for up to 3 - 5 days. To reheat, it's recommended you separate the crackling. Reheat meat in microwave, and crackling in a hot oven to retain crispiness. You can also slice and pan fry, or eat at room temperature on sandwiches or salads.

5. Nutrition information - The calculation assumes all fat including discarded rendered out fat is counted. Real calorie values are lower! But this is not a diet food, to be sure

Cooking

Garlic Braised Short Ribs With Red Wine

By Alison Roman

YIELD 6 servings
TIME About 4 1/2 hours

If you weren't already sure about how easy and delicious braised short ribs can be, consider this classic and straightforward recipe an excellent gateway. The ultimate hands-off, do-ahead dinner, these are done on the stovetop in a large Dutch oven but can easily be adapted to a slow cooker if that's your thing. When purchasing the ribs, ask for the thickest, meatiest ones available as they tend to shrink quite a bit once braised.

INGREDIENTS

2 tablespoons vegetable oil
5 pounds bone-in short ribs, at least 1 1/2 inches thick
Kosher salt and freshly ground pepper
2 large heads garlic, halved crosswise
1 medium onion (about 10 ounces), chopped
4 ribs celery (about 8 ounces), chopped
2 medium carrots (about 6 ounces), chopped
3 tablespoons tomato paste
2 cups dry red wine (about half a bottle)
2 cups beef stock or bone broth (use beef bouillon dissolved in water if unavailable; chicken stock will work in a pinch), plus more as needed
4 sprigs thyme
1 cup parsley, coarsely chopped
1/2 cup finely chopped chives
1 tablespoon finely grated lemon zest

PREPARATION

Step 1
Heat oven to 275 degrees. Heat oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high heat. Season short ribs on all sides with salt and pepper. Working in batches, sear short ribs on all sides until deeply and evenly browned, 6 to 8 minutes per batch. Transfer browned short ribs to a large plate and continue with remaining ribs.

Step 2
Pour off all but 2 tablespoons of remaining fat, leaving the good browned bits behind. Reduce heat to medium, and add garlic, cut side down and cook, undisturbed, until golden brown, about 1 to 2 minutes. Add onion, celery and carrots and season with salt and pepper. Toss to coat and continue to cook until vegetables are softened but not yet browned, about 5 to 10 minutes. Add tomato paste and stir to coat. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until tomato paste has started to caramelize a bit on the bottom and up the edges of the pot, about 2 to 3 minutes.

Step 3
Add red wine and, using a wooden spoon, scrape up any browned or caramelized bits. Let this simmer 2 to 3 minutes, just to take the edge off and reduce a bit. Stir in beef stock along with thyme. Using tongs, return short ribs to the pot, along with any juices that have accumulated, nestling them in there so that they are submerged (if they are just barely covered, nestle them bone side up so that all the meat is submerged, adding more beef stock or water as necessary to cover). Bring to a simmer, then cover and transfer to oven.

Step 4
Cook, undisturbed, until short ribs are meltingly tender and falling off the bone (you should be able to shred the meat with a fork), 3 1/2 to 4 hours.

Step 5
Using tongs, remove the ribs from the pot, taking care (for presentation purposes, really) not to let the bone slip out and transfer them to a large plate. (While you could serve the short ribs right out of this pot, the vegetables have all given up their flavor and texture and aren't worth much now, so feel free to strain the sauce for easier eating.) Scatter parsley, chives and lemon zest over the top of the short ribs. Separate the fat from the sauce, season with salt and pepper and serve alongside.

Zak Pelaccio's Crispy Pork and Watermelon Salad Recipe

There's a reason this Crispy Pork and Watermelon Salad is the signature dish at Zakary Pelaccio's Fatty Crab restaurants. It highlights the best of Pelaccio's cooking style, combining his love of Southeast Asian flavors with an irreverent American lean.

Not too many so-called salad recipes begin with slow braising pork belly, but that's kind of the best part of this one. Cool cubes of watermelon and pickled watermelon rind are tossed with deep fried chunks of pork belly, and finished off with torn leaves of Thai basil and Vietnamese mint. It's sweet and summery while having a round, porky richness that makes the salad totally irresistible. Oh, and take this salad outside, add a glass or two of off-dry Riesling and the cool sounds of Coltrane and you really can't go wrong.

Recommended playlist and drinks pairing:
Listen: Coltrane, Blue Train —the whole album; it never gets old.
Drink: Selbach-Oster Riesling Auslese 2005

What Worked: There's a reason this salad has been on the menu at Fatty Crab forever, it's a classic.

What Didn't: Pelaccio isn't shy with the chiles and if you subscribe to the same school of thought you might want to add sliced Thai chile or two to up the heat factor.

Suggested Tweaks: We could see this salad working equally well with mellow cantaloupe or even citrus segments.

Reprinted with permission from Eat with Your Hands by Zakary Pelaccio. Copyright © 2012. Published by Ecco. Available wherever books are sold. All rights reserved.

YIELD: serves 4 to 6   ACTIVE TIME: 1 hour   TOTAL TIME: 1 hour plus one day

Ingredients

For the Watermelon Salad
2 cups rice vinegar
3 shallots, thinly sliced
2 fresh Thai bird chilies, thinly sliced
2 fresh kaffir lime leaves
2 inches fresh ginger, peeled and sliced
1 1/2 ounces palm sugar (1 round gula jawa) or 2 tablespoons light brown sugar
1 tablespoon kosher salt
One 5-pound watermelon

For the Dressing
3 ounces palm sugar (2 rounds gula jawa) or 1/4 cup light brown sugar
1 cup rice vinegar
1/2 cup fresh lime juice
4 inches fresh ginger, peeled and sliced
6 fresh cilantro roots with 1 inch of stems, rinsed, scraped, and rinsed again, or 24 cilantro stems
2 garlic cloves, chopped
3/4 teaspoon kosher salt

For the Pork
About 3 cups rendered leaf lard or neutral oil, such as grapeseed or canola
2 pounds Braised Pork Belly (recipe follows), cut into 1-inch chunks while still cold
1 cup all-purpose flour
Sea salt

To finish the dish
1 cup fresh Vietnamese mint (rou ram) leaves
1 cup fresh Thai basil leaves
3 scallions, sliced
1/4 cup sesame seeds

Braised Pork Belly

For the Brine
1/4 cup coriander seeds
2 tablespoons fennel seeds
4 cups sea salt
2 cups sugar
10 garlic cloves, crushed and peeled
10 fresh long red chilies, such as Anaheim or Hungarian Wax, thinly sliced
5 medium shallots, sliced
3 tablespoons black peppercorns
1 cup packed daun salam (Indonesian bay leaves)
2 to 3 pounds fresh pork belly

For the Braise
2 tablespoons rendered leaf lard or olive oil (the best you can afford)
1 yellow onion, cut into sixths
1 head of garlic, halved crosswise
2 shallots, halved lengthwise
2 1/2 cups chicken stock

Directions

1. Brine the Pork Belly: Toast the coriander and fennel seeds in a dry pan over medium heat, swirling and shaking them until they crackle lightly and release their aroma, about 3 minutes. Set aside.
2. Combine the toasted seeds with the salt, sugar, garlic, chilies, shallots, peppercorns, daun salam, and 3 gallons water in a stockpot and bring to a boil over high heat. Reduce the heat and allow the brine to simmer for about 20 minutes. Remove the brine from the heat and let it come to room temperature, then refrigerate it. When it's completely cool, pour it over the belly and refrigerate, covered, for at least 24 and up to 48 hours.
3. Braise the Pork Belly: Preheat the oven to 225°F. Cut a piece of parchment paper to fit your roasting pan.
4. Remove the belly from the brine, rinse with cold water, and pat dry. Set aside.
5. In the roasting pan straddling two burners over medium-high, heat the leaf lard until hot but not smoking. Add the onion, garlic, and shallots, and cook, stirring occasionally, until golden and tender, 5 to 6 minutes. Add the stock to the pan and deglaze, scraping up any bits with a wooden spoon.
6. When the stock comes to a boil, add the belly to the roasting pan and remove it from the heat. Top the pan with the parchment paper and cover with a tight lid or foil.
7. Braise the belly in the oven until it is tender (when you press the tip of a pairing knife into it, there should be no resistance). Start checking it after 2. hours, though it could take up to 4 hours.
8. Remove the pan from the oven and let it sit at room temperature for 30 minutes.
9. Using two big spatulas or your hands, transfer the belly from the pan to a large plate or sheet tray and let it cool to room temperature. Strain the braising liquid and reserve for future use. The liquid can be stored in the fridge for up to 5 days or in the freezer for up to 3 months.
10. Wrap the belly tightly in plastic wrap. Press it between two flat pans (such as sheet trays) and put a weight on the top (a few cans of tomatoes will do the trick). Refrigerate, pressed, for at least 12 hours and up to 2 days.
11. After the belly has been cooked and pressed, it's ready for any of the following recipes or any other culinary purpose. It keeps in the fridge, wrapped tightly, for about 2 weeks or in the freezer for up to 6 months. To use frozen belly in a recipe, thaw it completely in the fridge first. Also, I like to cut my belly into portions prior to freezing so I don't have to thaw the whole megillah at once.
12. Make the Watermelon Salad: Combine everything for the salad except the watermelon in a small saucepan. Add 1 cup water, bring the liquid to a boil over medium heat, and cook, stirring, until the sugar dissolves.
13. Meanwhile, cut the rind from the watermelon flesh, reserving both the rind and the flesh. Use a sharp knife to pare away the outer, darker green skin, leaving the inner, whiter fleshy rind. Discard the darker green peel. Cut the white rind into 1/4-inch cubes and put them in a bowl. Strain the seasoned rice vinegar liquid over the diced rind. Let the mixture cool, then chill for at least 1 hour and up to 2 days.
14. Cut the flesh of the watermelon into 1-inch pieces (discarding whatever seeds you can). Chill it until you're ready to use it.
16. Fry the Pork In a large, straight-sided sauté pan or wok, heat 3 inches of lard to 375°F (measured on a deep-frying thermometer).
15. Make the Dressing: Roughly crush the palm sugar using a mortar and pestle or a plastic bag and a rolling pin. Pulse the sugar with the vinegar, lime juice, ginger, cilantro roots, garlic, and salt in a food processor until smooth and well combined.
17. Toss the cubed pork belly in the flour and shake off any excess. Working in batches, fry the pork belly until very crisp and a deep golden brown, 6 to 7 minutes. Transfer the pork with a slotted spoon to a paper-towel-lined tray to drain and season with salt. return the fat to 375°F between batches.
18. Finish the Salad: Tear the mint and basil leaves. In a mixing bowl, toss the pickled watermelon rind and the chilled watermelon flesh with the sliced scallions, mint, and basil. Add just enough dressing to coat. Divide the pork among the plates. Top with the salad and garnish each dish with a sprinkle of sesame seeds. Serve immediately.

title: Camca - Sumsa
description: Samsa is a staple savory pastry of Central Asian cuisine, traditionally baked in a tandoor but adapted here for a standard oven. The key to its signature flaky, multi-layered texture is the process of rolling the dough extremely thin, layering it with fat (melted butter), and chilling the resulting roll to ensure the layers remain distinct and crisp during the bake.
instructions: Knead the dough and let it rest for 30 minutes.
Divide the dough into 4 parts and shape them into balls.
Roll out each ball until it is very thin.
Brush each rolled-out layer with melted butter and stack all four layers on top of each other.
Press out any trapped air and roll the stacked layers into a tight log.
Cut the log into thin, equal pieces and flatten them out.
Place the pieces in the refrigerator for 1 hour.
Prepare the filling by mixing the finely chopped meat, onions, two potatoes, salt, spices, a bit of oil, and 50ml of sparkling water.
Make small balls and let them rest. Flatten each ball and put the filling in the center. Leave the edges clean. Pinch it like khinkali and leave a hole open.
Bake at 190°C (375°F) for 40 minutes.
notes: *Texture Control:* Do not skip the 1-hour refrigeration step; it hardens the butter between the layers, which is essential for achieving the spiral, flaky "puff" effect.
*Juiciness:* Finely chopping the meat by hand rather than using a grinder, combined with the addition of sparkling water, ensures the interior remains exceptionally juicy.

title: Satsivi for One Large Turkey
description: Satsivi is the crown jewel of Georgian festive cuisine, traditionally served cold during Christmas and New Year celebrations. The dish's unique chemistry relies on the high natural oil content of finely ground walnuts and a specific aromatic blend of warming spices, like blue fenugreek and marigold, which emulsify with the broth to create a rich, velvety sauce without the need for additional thickeners.
ingredients: Black Pepper: On the tip of a knife
Cloves: On the tip of a knife
Cinnamon: On the tip of a knife
Garlic: 4-5 cloves (processed in a food processor)
instructions: Boil the turkey separately.
Sauté a substantial amount of finely chopped onions in the fat rendered from the turkey broth.
Do not let the onions brown or burn; they should remain pale and soft.
Once the onions are ready, allow them to cool completely.
Move them into a blender.
While processing, gradually add walnuts and blended herbs to the blender.
Afterward, blend everything together witht the broth, determine the thickness by eye.
Keep in mind that the mixture will double or tripple in thickness after boiling.
Do not bring it to a full boil [too rapidly], otherwise it will curdle like cottage cheese.
As soon as it begins to simmer, stir it with a spoon.
Continue to stir in this manner until walnuts are boiled through.
Season with salt to taste; add more if necessary.
Finally, add a little white wine vinegar.
Stir, bring it to a boil once more, and then remove it from the heat.
Pour the hot sauce over an oven roasted turkey, cut into pieces ahead of a time
Cover the pot with the chese cloth, not a lid - otherwise it will "sweat" and will go bad/taste sour
notes: *Onions:* It is easier if the onions are processed in a food processor before sautéing
*Texture:* For the most authentic result, grind the walnuts until they are as fine as flour to ensure a completely smooth sauce.
*Onion Prep:* When sautéing the onions in the broth fat, keep the heat low to ensure they soften completely without caramelizing, which would alter the classic pale color of the sauce.
*Serving:* Satsivi must be prepared in advance and served cold or at room temperature to allow the walnut sauce to thicken naturally and the spices to fully bloom.

*Preventing Curdling:* To ensure the sauce does not "split" or take on a curdled, cottage-cheese-like texture, avoid a vigorous rolling boil. Maintain gentle heat and stir constantly once the mixture warms.
*Texture Cues:* The sauce naturally thickens as it cools; the recipe notes it will become twice as thick, so avoid over-reducing it while it is on the stove.

title: Indian Pudding
description: A classic New England baked cornmeal and molasses pudding, slow-baked for hours and served chilled with lightly whipped cream. The cold milk poured over the top before baking keeps the center soft.
ingredients: 1 quart plus 1/2 cup (1 L plus 120 ml) milk, divided
instructions: Heat oven to 300°F / 150°C. Butter the bottom and sides of a 9 x 9 inch baking dish.
Place 1 quart (1 L) milk in a saucepan or double boiler. Heat to about 180°F / 82°C, until small bubbles form at the edges, stirring frequently so it does not burn or form a skin.
In a bowl, whisk together the 1/2 cup cornmeal and 1 teaspoon salt.
When the milk reaches temperature, reduce heat to low. Slowly whisk in the cornmeal–salt mixture and cook for 10 minutes, stirring constantly.
Stir in 1/2 cup molasses; cook and stir for 2 minutes.
Stir in 1 1/2 teaspoons ginger or cinnamon (sift ground ginger to avoid clumps). Cook another 1 minute, until smooth.
Pour the hot batter into the prepared baking dish. Gently pour the remaining 1/2 cup (120 ml) cold milk over the top. Do not stir it in.
Bake for 3 to 4 hours. A darker top and a thin film/skin are normal.
Let the pudding cool completely so it firms up, up to 2 hours. Cover and refrigerate overnight or until completely chilled and set. Scoop into bowls, top with lightly whipped cream, and serve.
notes: *Skin:* Parchment paper pressed onto the surface while chilling prevents a thick skin; leave uncovered for the traditional "skin."

title: Choux Pastry (Shu)
description: This recipe details the preparation of "Shu," the classic Eastern European adaptation of French choux pastry. The technique relies on "scalding" flour in a mixture of boiling water and fat to gelatinize the starches, which creates a stable structure that traps steam during baking, allowing the dough to puff up into the iconic hollow shells used for profiteroles or eclairs. The second half of the recipe describes a traditional Soviet-style "zavarnoy" (cooked) custard, used to fill the Shu pastry. The core technique involves the gelatinization of flour starch to create a thick base, which is then enriched with butter and egg yolks for a silky, stable emulsion.
ingredients: 1 liter milk (pencil annotation on the card halves this to 0.5 l)
instructions: Boil the water and butter together until the butter is completely melted.
Remove the pot from the heat, add the flour, and mix it using a mixer.
Beat in the eggs one by one while mixing continuously with the mixer. Once you achieve a homogeneous mass, add a pinch of salt.
On a cold baking sheet (greased with a thin layer of fat), portion out the dough using a dessert spoon. Place them in a moderately hot oven and bake at moderate heat.
On a separate piece of paper, mix the sugar and flour so that they are distributed evenly.
Heat the milk, butter, and the flour-sugar mixture together and mix quickly with a mixer.
Lower the heat and, while stirring with a spoon, bring the cream to a thick consistency.
Cook until ready (until the raw flour taste disappears); at the end, add the vanilla and remove from the heat.
When it has cooled slightly, add 1–2 egg yolks and mix quickly with a mixer. Done!
Beat egg whites into a thick white mass and add it to the cream once it cools off.
No need to add sugar to the egg whites.
notes: *Temperature Control:* Ensure the water and butter reach a full boil before adding the flour to ensure proper starch gelatinization.
*Egg Incorporation:* Adding eggs one by one is crucial; the dough must fully absorb each egg before the next is added to maintain the correct "dropping" consistency.

To achieve a professional texture, ensure you cook the mixture long enough to eliminate any graininess or "floury" aftertaste. When adding the egg yolks, ensure the custard has cooled enough to prevent the eggs from scrambling, but remains warm enough to incorporate smoothly.

description: Gozinaki is a traditional Georgian New Year's confection made of walnuts and honey. Its success depends on carefully heating the honey to a specific concentration so that it binds the nuts into a crisp, snap-able brittle without scorching or losing its characteristic pale golden color.
instructions: Mix 1 tea cup of honey and 1 table spoon of sugar on low heat.
Keep stirring constantly with a spoon. Do not let it burn!
When you first place it on the stove, it will foam up, immediately remove it from the heat.
After a short while, place it back on low heat and bring it to a boil.
Test the readiness by dropping a bead into a glass of cold water to see how it falls.
Take 6 cups of un-chopped walnuts.
Cover them with the mixure and then cut them finely after it cools off.
notes: The cold water test is essential: the honey is ready when a drop forms a firm ball that does not dissolve in the water.
Removing the honey from the heat when it first foams prevents bitterness and maintains the light color.

description: This Georgian "Ideali" cake is a nostalgic walnut staple, prized for its deep caramelized flavor and soft, layered texture. title: '"Eskimo" Cake'
description: "Eskimo" cake is a beloved nostalgic dessert in Georgian cuisine, named for its resemblance to the creamy texture and chocolate coating of a classic ice cream bar. The recipe relies on a dual-part cream, a cooked custard folded into whipped buttercream, and a light sponge leavened by the chemical reaction of vinegar and baking soda combined with aerated egg whites.
instructions: Whisk the 4 egg yolks with 300g of sugar until pale. Add the milk, sour cream, flour, baking soda, and walnuts. In a separate bowl, whisk the 4 egg whites, then gently fold them into the dough. Bake on buttered parchment paper at a low heat.
To make the custard (Part I), combine 4 egg yolks, 1.5 cups of sugar, 3 tablespoons of flour, and 0.5 liters of milk. Cook the mixture over heat (boil) until thickened.
To make the buttercream (Part II), whisk 250g of butter with 200g of sugar and vanilla until fluffy.
Once the custard (Part I) has cooled completely, whisk it into the buttercream (Part II).

Combine 1 cup of sugar, 2 tablespoons of cocoa, 6 tablespoons of milk, and 100g of butter. Bring the mixture to a boil while stirring constantly. Once the glaze has cooled slightly, brush it over the finished cake.
notes: Ensure the custard base is completely cooled to room temperature before mixing it with the whipped butter to prevent the cream from curdling or melting. For the sponge, bake at a low temperature (approximately 325°F/160°C) to maintain a soft, light texture without drying it out.

instructions: *Prepare the Starter (Opara):* In a separate bowl, combine 1 L of warm milk with 2 tablespoons of sugar, flour, and yeast. Mixure should have the consistency of Oladiki dough. Wrap the bowl warmly and allow to rise. Once risen, add into the main mixure

Brush the top with egg yolk before baking

notes: *Temperature Control:* The milk used for the yeast starter must be warm, never hot, or it will kill the yeast.

*Spices:* For the best flavor, let your spices sit in cognac or alcohol before adding them to the dough.
To ensure the best results, avoid applying an excessive amount of egg yolk to the top of the dough, as this can lead to burning.

title: Homemade Granola
description: A big-batch toasted granola loaded with coconut, almonds, cashews, and four kinds of dried fruit. Printed from FoodNetwork.com, inspired by Sarah Chase's Open House Cookbook; makes 12 cups.
instructions: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F.

Toss the oats, coconut, and almonds together in a large bowl. Whisk together the oil and honey in a small bowl. Pour the liquids over the oat mixture and stir with a wooden spoon until all the oats and nuts are coated.
Pour onto a 13 by 18 by 1-inch sheet pan. Bake, stirring occasionally with a spatula, until the mixture turns a nice, even, golden brown, about 45 minutes.
Remove the granola from the oven and allow to cool, stirring occasionally. Add the apricots, figs, cherries, cranberries, and cashews. Store the cooled granola in an airtight container.
notes: *Timing:* Prep 15 min; cook 45 min; makes 12 cups.
